intro.html: Some people notice everything; some notice nothing. These words describe both, and the steps in between: taking something in through the senses (perceive), telling things apart (discern), understanding something deep (fathom) and gathering facts a little at a time (glean). The adjectives describe watchful people (vigilant, wary), aware people (cognizant) and people who miss what is right in front of them (oblivious, heedless).
Paying attention: perceive, discern, vigilant, wary, cognizant. Not paying attention: oblivious, heedless. Hard to notice: subtle.

words.def: to notice or become aware of, through the senses or the mind
words.ex: Owls can {perceive} the tiny rustle of a mouse in the grass.
words.ctx: At first the change was too small to {perceive}, but after a month everyone could see that the little tree had grown taller than the fence.
words.etym: From Latin percipere, “to take hold of completely”: per (thoroughly) + capere (to take).

mn.text: Sami peers into the night sky and receives a tiny flash of light: a shooting star! To {perceive} is to take in something with your senses.

scene.alt: A boy with a telescope spots a shooting star in the night sky.

words.def: to notice or tell apart, often with effort
words.ex: In the fog, Dad could barely {discern} the outline of the barn.
words.ctx: The twins look alike to strangers, but their friends can easily {discern} which is which: Mia always tilts her head when she listens.
words.etym: From Latin discernere, “to separate, tell apart”: dis (apart) + cernere (to sift).

mn.text: Two gems look exactly alike, but Ada’s sharp eye can tell that this one is real and that one is glass. To {discern} is to tell things apart.

scene.alt: A woman studies two identical-looking gems with a magnifying glass to tell the real one from the fake.

words.def: to understand something fully, after much thought
words.ex: Pip could not {fathom} why anyone would put pineapple on a pancake.
words.ctx: Scientists are still trying to {fathom} how the birds find their way home across thousands of miles of open ocean.
words.etym: From Old English fæðm, “outstretched arms”; a fathom became a unit of six feet for measuring the depth of water, and to fathom came to mean to get to the bottom of something.
words.note: Often used with “can’t”: I can’t fathom why he left.

mn.cue: FATHOM: get to the BOTTOM of it
mn.text: Sailors once lowered a weighted rope to find the depth of the sea in fathoms. To {fathom} a mystery is to get all the way to the bottom of it.

scene.alt: A sailor in a rowboat lowers a rope to measure the depth of the sea while a whale swims nearby.

words.def: to gather information bit by bit
words.ex: From the muddy paw prints, Lila {gleaned} that the dog had been in the garden.
words.ctx: The reporter could not interview the mayor, so she {gleaned} what she could from old speeches, news clips and a few chats with neighbors.
words.etym: From Old French glener, “to gather grain left behind after the harvest”; the sense of gathering facts came later.

mn.cue: GLEAN = CLEAN UP every last bit
mn.text: After the harvest, Nana Lou walks the field and picks up every last stalk the reapers missed. In the same way, a careful reader can {glean} facts bit by bit.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a straw hat gathers the last bits of the harvest into a basket.

words.ex: The hikers were {cognizant} of the park’s bear rules because they had read every sign at the trailhead.
words.ctx: The new principal was {cognizant} of the school’s problems before she arrived; she had read every report and talked with dozens of parents.
words.etym: From cognizance, from Old French conoissance, “knowledge,” from Latin cognoscere, “to get to know.”
words.note: Usually followed by “of”: cognizant of the risk.

mn.cue: reCOGNIZE-ant: you recognize what is going on
mn.text: Dev recognizes the cracked ice and the warning sign, so he stays on the shore. He is {cognizant} of the danger.

scene.alt: A teen in winter clothes points at a thin ice warning sign and stays off the frozen pond.

words.def: watchful and alert for danger or trouble
words.ex: The {vigilant} lifeguard never took her eyes off the water and spotted the struggling swimmer in seconds.
words.ctx: During the dry summer, rangers stayed {vigilant}, climbing the fire tower every hour to scan the hills for the first wisp of smoke.
words.etym: From Latin vigilare, “to stay awake, keep watch,” from vigil (awake).

mn.cue: a VIGIL: awake and watching all night
mn.text: All night long the old owl keeps a vigil over the henhouse, eyes wide open, watching for foxes. She is {vigilant}.

scene.alt: A wide-eyed owl on a fence keeps watch at night and spots a sneaking fox.

words.def: cautious about possible danger or trickery
words.ex: The stray cat was {wary} of strangers but loved the girl who fed it.
words.ctx: Burned once by a deal that sounded too good to be true, Grandpa was {wary} of the smooth salesman and asked to see everything in writing.
words.note: Wary (cautious) is not weary (tired). A weary hiker wants to rest; a wary hiker watches for bears.

mn.text: A sign says “Beware of the goose,” so Kai tiptoes past the pond, watching the goose every step. He is {wary}.

scene.alt: A boy tiptoes cautiously past an angry goose and a beware of goose sign.

words.def: not aware of what is happening around you
words.ex: Lost in her book, Maya was {oblivious} to the rain soaking her shoes.
words.ctx: The tourists were so busy taking pictures that they were {oblivious} to the sign warning that the tide was coming in fast.
words.etym: From Latin obliviosus, “forgetful,” from oblivisci, “to forget.”
words.note: Followed by “to” or “of”: oblivious to the noise.

mn.text: Felix bobs his head to the songs in his headphones, “Oh, bliss!”, while the dog trots off with his sandwich. He is {oblivious}.

scene.alt: A man listening to music on a bench does not notice a dog running off with his sandwich.

words.def: paying no attention to warnings or dangers; careless
words.ex: {Heedless} of the wet-paint sign, Pip plopped down on the bench and ruined his shorts.
words.ctx: The young pilot was not brave but {heedless}: he ignored every storm warning and flew straight into the thunderclouds.

mn.text: Pip pays no heed to the “Wet Paint” sign and sits right down on the bench. He is {heedless}.

scene.alt: A boy happily sits on a freshly painted bench, ignoring the wet paint sign.

words.def: so slight or delicate that it is hard to notice
words.ex: The soup had a {subtle} hint of lemon.
words.ctx: The change in the painting was {subtle}; only an expert noticed that one tiny boat had been moved from the left side of the harbor to the right.
words.etym: From Latin subtilis, “fine, thin, precise.” The b was added to the English spelling to match the Latin and was never pronounced.

mn.text: The b in subtle makes no sound at all, so you hardly notice it is there. A difference that slight is {subtle}.

scene.alt: An old professor peers through a magnifying glass, comparing two nearly identical paintings.

after.html: Wary and weary differ by one letter. Wary means cautious; weary means tired. Oblivious takes “to” or “of”: oblivious to the noise, oblivious of the time.

items.q: After hiking all day, the ______ campers fell asleep at once. Which word fits?
items.why: Weary means tired. Wary (cautious) and vigilant (watchful) do not explain falling asleep at once.

choices: Absorbed in his game, he was oblivious to the doorbell.
She was oblivious of danger, so she checked every lock twice.
The oblivious guard noticed the tiny scratch on the vault.
He was oblivious, so he heard every word of the whisper.
items.why: Oblivious means unaware. Only the first sentence describes someone who does not notice something.

items.q: Type the adjective, spelled with a silent letter, that means “so slight it is hard to notice.”
True or false: a heedless driver pays close attention to every warning sign.
items.why: False. Heed means attention; heedless means without attention, careless.
